item.title: Six big takeaways from a turbulent week of UN diplomacy
item.description:
By Antoni Slodkowski

UNITED NATIONS, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Limousines whisked world leaders away from the United Nations on Friday after a week of speeches, meetings and hallway diplomacy.

While they reached no breakthroughs on the world's most intractable conflicts, talks on the Iran and Ukraine wars inched forward and global powers used the venue to debate AI risks with industry leaders.

Here are the big takeaways from scores of panels, hundreds of meetings, hours spent in lines and listening to speeches – and countless cups of coffee:

REBOOT OF IRAN DIPLOMACY

item.title: Iran awaits US move after WSJ report says Trump rejects peace plan
item.description:
By Menna AlaaElDin and Parisa Hafezi

CAIRO/UNITED NATIONS, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Iran on Saturday awaited a US response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East war after the Wall Street Journal reported that President Donald Trump had rejected the deal.

Iran raised the diplomatic initiative at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators and could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within sevendays.

item.title: Iran proposes Hormuz plan, Trump reportedly refuses
item.description:
The United States had yet to publicly respond on Saturday after Iran offered a plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, though reports indicated that President Donald Trump had rejected the proposal.

The waterway key to the world's oil supply is central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which is at a stalemate after nearly seven months, though new mediation efforts took place this week.

item.title: Iran proposes plan to reopen Hormuz within seven days: minister
item.description:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that Tehran had offered Washington a plan that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened to maritime navigation within seven days once agreed.

Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel.

item.title: Pakistani, Saudi, Turkish chiefs discuss closer military ties
item.description:
Sept 26 (Reuters) - The military chiefs of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey discussed enhancing intelligence sharing, military coordination and capability integration at a meeting in Riyadh on Friday, according to statements from Saudi Arabia's Defence Ministry and Pakistan's military.

The chiefs of defence forces and chiefs of general staff reviewed the security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia and condemned attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis targeting the holy city of Makkah as well as the kingdom's civilian and economic infrastructure, the statements said.

item.title: Iran's Araqchi says now up to US to accept 7-day plan
item.description:
Sept 25 (Reuters) - Iran has given the United States a "concrete" seven-day plan to open the strategic Strait of Hormuz and the choice now rests with the US, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday.

"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States," he said.

item.title: Despite fanfare, Xi shows Trump no sign of breaking with Iran
item.description: Beijing has significant leverage over Tehran, but little incentive to use it for Washington’s benefit, given its reliance on Iranian oil.

item.title: Pakistan PM calls Houthi Mecca attacks 'red line' at UN
item.description:
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said at the UN Friday that further attacks on the Islamic holy city of Mecca would be a "red line" for Islamabad.

Pakistan maintains ties with Iran which backs the Houthi fighters responsible for firing missiles at Saudi Arabia where Mecca is situated.

But Islamabad is strategically close to Saudi, and entered into a defense agreement with the kingdom, and Turkey, last month.

item.title: Could Iran's 7-day Hormuz proposal culminate in diplomatic deal?
item.description: Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days brings into focus the central challenge facing diplomacy with Washington: how to turn military leverage into a negotiated path without giving up too much in return.

item.title: Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
item.description:
By Parisa Hafezi and Don Durfee

UNITED NATIONS, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.

The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until “all of Iran’s conditions are met” by the United States.

item.title: Subway, soccer and spats: New York's Mamdani a UN week attraction
item.description:
By Michelle Nichols

UNITED NATIONS, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The United Nations wasn't the only New York attraction for visiting world leaders this week – MayorZohran Mamdani emerged as a popular draw for like-minded politicians and a target for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

item.title: UN Security Council condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
item.description:
The United Nations Security Council on Friday condemned escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemeni Houthi fighters in a rare show of unity from the UN's top body.

The Houthis have imposed a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, hitting its tankers, seizing swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast vital for oil exports and causing energy prices to jump, while also raining missiles on the kingdom.

item.title: Trump, Xi end summit with tea, tour of US archives - and little sign of progress
item.description:
By Steve Holland and David Brunnstrom

WASHINGTON, Sept 25 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping drank tea at the White House and visited the National Archives on Friday, ending a three-day summit that showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs on a host of contentious issues.

Trump said "our farmers are going to be happy" as a result of the talks but did not provide details.

"America is very happy about this visit, and I'm sureChina is very happy also," he said.

item.title: What France’s military deployment means for Saudi Arabia’s fight against Houthis
item.description: New pledges of limited British and French military deployments fall short of what Riyadh would likely need to defend its skies should the Houthis escalate further.
